opus-5.5.text:
So I think the cleanest way to see it is that the policy network gives you a prior: a fast, intuitive guess at which moves look good. That's like a strong player glancing at the board. Monte Carlo tree search is what turns that intuition into something closer to calculated confidence.

When you run the search, you spend compute exploring the consequences of each candidate move. You expand the tree, evaluate positions with the value network, and back those estimates up to the root. The visit counts you end up with are a sharpened version of the prior. Moves that held up under scrutiny get visited more, and moves that looked attractive but fell apart a few plies deep get abandoned. So the distribution after search should be more peaked and more correct than the raw policy.

The key insight from AlphaGo Zero, and the reason it works as a self-improvement loop, is that you then train the policy to match those post-search visit counts. Search acts as a policy improvement operator. You're distilling the slow, deliberate reasoning back into fast intuition, so the next round of search starts from a better prior and can look even deeper.

There are some subtleties. Search shouldn't make you blindly overconfident. If you only run a handful of simulations, the visit counts are noisy, so how much you trust the result should scale with how much compute you spent. And there's the exploration term: you deliberately keep some probability mass on moves the network underrates, because otherwise you can never find out that your prior was wrong. That's why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise at the root during self-play.

What I find interesting is how much of this carries over to language models now. Sampling many reasoning chains, verifying them, and reinforcing the ones that work is structurally similar. You're using test-time compute to produce a better answer than the model's first instinct, then folding that back into the weights. The hard part outside of games is that you don't have a perfect simulator or a clean win/loss signal, so your value estimates are much shakier. Getting that value function right is where a lot of the real difficulty lives.

r001.rationale: The response says search visit counts are more peaked than the raw policy and that confidence should scale with compute, but it does not state that increasing the number of simulations increasingly concentrates the action distribution on a preferred move.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that tree search is basically a way of spending compute to sharpen a prior. Your policy network gives you some distribution over moves, and that's its gut feeling. Search is you going "okay, let me actually imagine what happens if I play this," and the result of that imagination should move your confidence, but in a pretty specific way.

The first thing is that the amount the search should change your mind depends on how good your value estimates are at the leaves. If your value function is garbage, then rolling out ten thousand simulations just gives you very confident garbage. People sometimes treat visit counts as if they're calibrated probabilities, and they're not. They're more like "how much did the search want to keep looking here." So I'd say search should increase confidence in proportion to how much the search agrees with itself as you deepen it. If you double the simulation budget and the move distribution barely moves, that's a signal you've converged on something real. If it keeps flipping, you should actually be less confident than the raw policy was, because the position is telling you it's sharp and your prior didn't know that.

The second thing, and this is the part I find more interesting, is that the delta between the policy prior and the post-search distribution is itself information. In AlphaZero that gap is literally the training signal. But at inference time it also tells you how surprised you should be. If search massively overturns your prior, either you found a tactic the network couldn't see, which is great, or your value function is being exploited by some weird branch of the tree. And you can't tell those two apart from inside the search. So I'd argue the right posture is that a big disagreement should raise your confidence in the move but lower your confidence in your own model of the position.

And then the thing I think gets undersold is that in the real world, unlike Go, you often don't have a perfect simulator. So MCTS in a learned world model is compounding errors with depth. Deep lines should get discounted not because the discount factor says so but because your imagination gets blurrier the farther out you go. A system that's actually calibrated would treat a twenty-step rollout in a learned model as weaker evidence than a five-step one, even if the twenty-step one is reporting a higher value. Most implementations don't do that, and I think that's where a lot of the overconfidence comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says search can sharpen a policy prior and that stability as simulations increase signals convergence, but it does not state that more simulations make the action distribution increasingly concentrated on a preferred action.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to think about it is that your policy gives you an initial guess about which move is best, and search gives you a way to revise that guess by spending more computation. You might initially favor one move, but when you explore the consequences, you discover that it gives your opponent a really strong response. So you shift toward another move.

But search shouldn’t necessarily make you more confident. Sometimes it reveals that the decision is much closer than you thought. And if all your evaluations share the same blind spot, running more simulations can make you more confident without making you more correct. The benefit comes from discovering something about the possible futures that your initial judgment didn’t capture, not just from repeatedly confirming that judgment.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that more MCTS simulations concentrate the action distribution on a preferred move. It says search can shift the preference or reveal that the decision is closer, and that more simulations may increase confidence without improving correctness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to think about it is that search gives you additional evidence about the moves you were initially uncertain about. Your policy might initially put a lot of probability on one move, but when you actually explore the consequences, you might discover that it leads to a bad position. So you should become less confident in that move and shift probability toward something else.

But there’s a subtlety: running more simulations doesn’t necessarily mean you should become more confident. Sometimes thinking longer reveals that the decision is harder than you thought. Ideally, search lets you distinguish between “I like this move because it looks familiar” and “I like this move because I’ve examined the alternatives and it holds up.”

r001.rationale: The candidate says that running more simulations does not necessarily increase confidence and discusses shifting probability after exploring alternatives. It does not state that additional MCTS simulations increasingly concentrate the action distribution on a preferred action.
